info.title: Cloud World Model — Agent API
info.description: Agent-facing API surface for Cloud World Model. Includes free lifecycle operations (create/inspect simulations, list scenarios, poll job status) and 40 x402-priced endpoints spanning simulation execution, RL training, chaos engineering, multi-cloud analysis, AI explanations, and infrastructure validation. 24 of those endpoints are directly indexable by x402 crawlers (cold-probeable without a prior resource ID); the remaining 16 are resource-scoped status and results endpoints that require an existing job or simulation ID. Anonymous callers can pay per request with USDC on Base (x402 protocol) — no account or API key required.

post.summary: Request an EIP-191 sign-in challenge
post.description:
Issues a one-time nonce for the given EVM wallet address. The caller must
sign the returned `message` string with `personal_sign` (EIP-191) and
submit the hex signature to `POST /wallet-auth/verify` within 5 minutes.

Rate-limited to 10 requests per IP per minute to prevent nonce-farming.
No authentication required.

walletAddress.description: The EVM wallet address requesting a sign-in challenge

nonce.description: The random hex nonce (32 hex chars)

message.description: The full message string to sign with personal_sign
message.example:
Sign in to Cloud World Model
Nonce: a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6
Expires: 2026-01-01T00:05:00.000Z

expiresAt.description: ISO-8601 timestamp when the nonce expires (5 minutes)

429.description: Rate limit exceeded — 10 challenges per IP per minute

post.summary: Verify an EIP-191 signature and receive a session token
post.description:
Verifies the EIP-191 personal_sign signature for the challenge previously
issued by `POST /wallet-auth/challenge`. On success, returns a 24-hour
JWT session token.

Use the token as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on `GET /simulations`
and `GET /simulations/{simulationId}` to list and retrieve simulations
claimed by this wallet address without a traditional API key.

The nonce is single-use and consumed on successful verification.
No authentication required.

walletAddress.description: The EVM wallet address that signed the challenge

signature.description: Hex-encoded EIP-191 signature from personal_sign (0x-prefixed, 65 bytes)

post.summary: Issue a wallet session JWT via x402 micro-payment
post.description:
Issues a 24-hour wallet session JWT in exchange for a small USDC
micro-payment on Base (x402 protocol).  Designed for managed/MPC
wallets that cannot sign EIP-191 challenges directly.

**Flow:**
1. Call this endpoint with no `X-PAYMENT` header — the server returns
   `402 Payment Required` with the USDC amount and payment details.
2. Submit the x402 payment and resend the request with the
   `X-PAYMENT` header populated.
3. On success the response body includes both a `settlement` block
   (confirmed transaction hash) and a `walletSession` block
   containing the JWT token and its expiry.

The issuance is idempotent per transaction hash — replaying the same
transaction hash returns the same session: the returned token carries
the same `jti` (session nonce) as the original issuance. No new
session record is created. The token's `iat`/`exp` timestamps differ
between calls (each JWT is freshly signed), but the session identity
bound by `jti` is stable across all replays of the same hash.

**Token lifetime and persistence:** Tokens are valid for 24 hours and
reusable across requests until they expire. Token validity **survives
server restarts only when the `WALLET_AUTH_JWT_SECRET` environment
variable is set to a stable, persistent value**. Without it, an
ephemeral per-process secret is used and all sessions are invalidated
on every redeploy. The server logs a startup warning when this variable
is absent.

**Authentication:** x402 micro-payment only (no API key required).

200.description: Session JWT issued alongside x402 settlement

walletSession.description:
Issued wallet session JWT (24-hour TTL). Tokens are reusable
across requests until expiry. Token validity survives server
restarts only when the `WALLET_AUTH_JWT_SECRET` environment
variable is set to a stable, persistent value — without it
sessions are invalidated on every redeploy.

token.description: JWT session token (HS256, 24-hour TTL, reusable until expiry)

get.summary: Discover x402 pricing and payment config
get.description:
Returns the x402 payment configuration for this server, including the USDC-on-Base
wallet address, network, asset contract, facilitator URL, and per-call-type price table.

AI agents can use this endpoint to discover whether x402 anonymous pay-per-request is
enabled, and to obtain the exact USDC amounts required before sending a `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE`
header on a metered endpoint.

This endpoint requires no authentication and is always public.

simulationRetentionDays.description:
Number of days an x402-wallet-owned simulation is retained after its
last activity (step, update). Every `/step-hybrid` call on a simulation
resets this rolling window. After the window expires, the simulation and
all its metrics are permanently deleted by the server's cleanup sweep.

post.summary: Create a cloud simulation
post.description:
Creates a simulation with cloud resources (compute, network, database, storage).
The simulation serves as the environment for RL training.

**Ownership:** If an `Authorization: Bearer <key>` header is provided, the
new simulation is immediately assigned to that API key and is fully write-accessible
without any additional steps. Without authentication the simulation is created
as a "demo" simulation (`apiKeyId: null`), subject to a 20-step limit; use
`POST /simulations/{simulationId}/claim` to adopt it once you have a key.

get.summary: List simulations for the authenticated caller
get.description:
Returns simulations owned by the authenticated caller.

**API key callers:** Returns all simulations assigned to the API key.
Admin-scoped keys receive all simulations across all keys.

**Wallet session callers:** Returns simulations claimed by the wallet
address (where `ownerWallet` matches), paginated via `limit` and `offset`
query parameters and sorted by `updatedAt` descending. The response shape
differs — it is an object `{ simulations, total, limit, offset }` rather
than a plain array.

Requires `read` scope or a valid wallet session JWT.

post.summary: Create an RL training environment
post.description:
Creates a reinforcement learning environment for training agents.
Links to an existing simulation and configures episode parameters.

This endpoint works with simulations built on **any supported provider**,
including AWS, GCP, Azure, OCI, and **DigitalOcean**. Training an agent against
a DigitalOcean simulation lets you learn optimal autoscaling strategies for
Droplet-based workloads, Managed Database failover handling, and
multi-datacenter traffic routing — all without incurring real cloud costs.
The observation space, action space, and reward function are identical
regardless of provider.

**Idle TTL:** Authenticated RL environments expire after **2 hours of inactivity**
(no `step` or `reset` call received). Expired environments and their linked
simulations are removed automatically; subsequent requests return `404`. Reset the
idle timer by calling `POST /rl/environments/{environmentId}/step` or
`POST /rl/environments/{environmentId}/reset` at least once every 2 hours during
long training runs.

**Note:** In-memory deployments (the default) do not persist RL environments
across server restarts. Reconnect or recreate the environment after a restart.

**UI Status Viewer:** Once an environment is running you can monitor its episodes,
cumulative rewards, and health without writing code — open the
[RL Environment Status viewer](/admin/rl-environments) in the platform UI and enter
your API key to see all active environments at a glance.

digitalOceanWaveTraffic.description:
Train an agent on a DigitalOcean simulation using a wave traffic pattern.
The simulationId must reference an existing simulation that contains
DigitalOcean resources (Droplets, Managed Database, Load Balancer).

digitalOceanBurstTraffic.summary: DigitalOcean Droplet cluster — burst traffic with failure injection
digitalOceanBurstTraffic.description:
More challenging episode: burst traffic spikes combined with random failure
injection (e.g., Managed Database failover). Useful for training a robust
agent that can handle both scaling pressure and partial outages.

digitalOceanAMDNVMe.summary: DigitalOcean AMD NVMe Droplet cluster — sustained ramp traffic
digitalOceanAMDNVMe.description:
Train an agent on a DigitalOcean simulation using AMD NVMe Droplets
(s-2vcpu-4gb-amd). The AMD variant uses NVMe-backed local storage and
AMD EPYC processors, offering lower per-hour cost than equivalent
Intel Droplets while delivering comparable CPU performance for
compute-bound workloads.

The cost budget of $2.80/hr reflects typical pricing for two
s-2vcpu-4gb-amd Droplets plus a single Managed PostgreSQL basic node
in nyc3. Use this example to benchmark agent policies across Intel vs.
AMD Droplet fleets under a sustained ramp traffic pattern.

awsSpot.summary: AWS EC2 Spot — cost-optimized batch RL training using Spot Instances
awsSpot.description:
Train an agent on a cost-sensitive AWS workload backed by EC2 Spot Instances.
The simulationId must reference an existing simulation containing Spot-eligible
resources (e.g. t3.xlarge or c5.2xlarge instances). The cost budget of $1.80/hr
reflects typical Spot pricing for a small fleet of t3.large instances in us-east-1
(roughly 70% below on-demand list price). Latency SLA is relaxed to 500 ms p95
to accommodate the occasional Spot interruption and re-scheduling delay. Use this
example to benchmark agent policies that prioritise cost efficiency over strict
latency guarantees — a common requirement for ML training, data pipelines, and
other fault-tolerant batch workloads.

gcpSpot.summary: GCP Spot VM — cost-optimized batch RL training using preemptible compute
gcpSpot.description:
Train an agent on a cost-sensitive GCP workload backed by Spot VMs (formerly
preemptible). The simulationId must reference an existing simulation containing
Spot-eligible resources (e.g. n2-standard-4 or c2-standard-8 Spot instances in
us-central1). The cost budget of $1.60/hr reflects typical Spot pricing for a
small fleet of n2-standard-4 instances (roughly 70% below on-demand list price).
Latency SLA is relaxed to 500 ms p95 to accommodate the occasional preemption
and re-scheduling delay. Use this example to benchmark agent policies that
prioritise cost efficiency over strict latency guarantees — ideal for ML
training, data processing, and other fault-tolerant batch workloads on GCP.

azureSpot.summary: Azure Spot VM — cost-optimized batch RL training using Azure Spot instances
azureSpot.description:
Train an agent on a cost-sensitive Azure workload backed by Azure Spot VMs.
The simulationId must reference an existing simulation containing Spot-eligible
resources (e.g. Standard_D4s_v3 or Standard_F8s_v2 Spot instances in eastus).
The cost budget of $1.50/hr reflects typical Spot pricing for a small fleet of
Standard_D4s_v3 instances (roughly 70% below pay-as-you-go list price). Latency
SLA is relaxed to 400 ms p95 to accommodate Azure Spot eviction and re-deployment
delays. Use this example to benchmark agent policies that prioritise cost
efficiency over strict latency guarantees — well-suited for batch inference,
data pipelines, and other interruption-tolerant workloads on Azure.

ociPreemptible.summary: OCI Ampere A1 Preemptible — cost-optimized batch RL training using OCI preemptible compute
ociPreemptible.description:
Train an agent on a cost-sensitive OCI workload backed by preemptible Ampere A1
instances. The simulationId must reference an existing simulation containing
preemptible-eligible resources (e.g. VM.Standard.A1.Flex instances in
us-ashburn-1). OCI preemptible instances are priced at roughly 50% below
standard on-demand rates, making them the most cost-effective option in OCI for
fault-tolerant batch workloads. The cost budget of $1.20/hr reflects typical
preemptible pricing for a small Ampere A1 fleet. Latency SLA is relaxed to
600 ms p95 to accommodate the occasional preemption and re-scheduling delay.
Use this example to benchmark agent policies that prioritise cost efficiency
over strict latency guarantees — ideal for ML training, data pipelines,
genomic workloads, and other interruption-tolerant tasks on OCI.

post.summary: Advance simulation one step (hybrid ML + rules)
post.description:
Steps the simulation using the Hybrid Prediction Engine, which blends a
deterministic rule-based simulation with a simulated ML-based prediction.
The engine uses a confidence threshold to decide how much weight to give
each path, and falls back to pure rules when ML confidence is low.

Returns the updated simulation state, step metrics, events, the hybrid
decision record (including ML confidence and blending rationale), and the
updated cumulative hybrid result object.

Requires `write` scope and ownership.

Python – warm-up/training
x-codeSamples.source:
"""
Two-phase training loop: fast warm-up followed by fine-grained training.

Phase 1 – Warm-up (300 s ticks)
  Use large tick_seconds to fast-forward through startup noise before the
  agent starts making meaningful autoscaling decisions. Each step advances
  the simulation clock by 5 minutes, so 20 warm-up steps cover ~1.7 hours
  of simulated time in seconds of wall time.

Phase 2 – Training (60 s ticks)
  Switch to 1-minute ticks for precise autoscaling control. The agent now
  observes and reacts to traffic on a per-minute basis, matching the
  granularity of real autoscaling cooldown windows (e.g. AWS default: 300 s).
"""
import requests

BASE_URL = "https://your-production-domain.com/api"
API_KEY = "your-api-key"
ENV_ID = "env-aws-001"

session = requests.Session()
session.headers.update({"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"})

def step(action: dict, tick_seconds: int) -> dict:
    resp = session.post(
        f"{BASE_URL}/rl/environments/{ENV_ID}/step",
        json={"action": action, "tick_seconds": tick_seconds},
    )
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()

NO_OP = {"type": "no_op", "parameters": {}}

WARMUP_STEPS = 20
print("=== Warm-up phase (300 s ticks) ===")
for i in range(WARMUP_STEPS):
    data = step(NO_OP, tick_seconds=300)
    print(
        f"  warmup {i+1:2d}/{WARMUP_STEPS}  "
        f"sim={data['sim_time_human']:>8s}  "
        f"cpu={data['obs']['cpu_util']:.1%}  "
        f"instances={data['obs']['instances']}"
    )
    if data["done"]:
        print("  Episode ended during warm-up — reset and retry.")
        break

print("\n=== Training phase (60 s ticks) ===")
done = False
while not done:
    cpu = data["obs"]["cpu_util"]
    if cpu > 0.75:
        action = {"type": "scale_out", "parameters": {"instanceCount": 1}}
    elif cpu < 0.30 and data["obs"]["instances"] > 1:
        action = {"type": "scale_in", "parameters": {"instanceCount": 1}}
    else:
        action = NO_OP

    data = step(action, tick_seconds=60)
    done = data["done"]
    print(
        f"  t={data['t']:4d}  sim={data['sim_time_human']:>8s}  "
        f"reward={data['reward']:+.3f}  "
        f"cpu={data['obs']['cpu_util']:.1%}  "
        f"p95={data['metrics']['latency_p95']} ms  "
        f"cost=${data['metrics']['cost_usd_hr']:.2f}/hr  "
        f"done={done}"
    )

Python – mid-episode cold instance (warmup_factor)
x-codeSamples.source:
"""
Mid-episode warmup_factor safe-access pattern.

obs.warmup_factor is an optional field — it is ABSENT from the observation
vector until the first cold compute instance exists in the episode. This happens
in two cases:
  1. An `add_resource` action provisions a new compute resource mid-episode.
  2. Canvas autoscaling adds a compute replica in response to high CPU/traffic.

Because the field appears dynamically, agents building a fixed-width
observation vector must default to 1.0 (fully warmed) when the field is absent:

  wf = obs.get("warmup_factor", 1.0)

A value < 1.0 means at least one compute instance is still warming up and is
not yet at full throughput. Use wf directly as a feature — do not re-derive it
from step counters or metrics.compute[].warmup_steps_remaining.

The pattern below shows a typical episode loop that handles both the pre-warmup
phase (field absent) and the post-add_resource warm-up window (field in (0, 1]).
"""
import requests

BASE_URL = "https://your-production-domain.com/api"
API_KEY = "your-api-key"
ENV_ID = "env-aws-001"

session = requests.Session()
session.headers.update({"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"})

def step(action: dict) -> dict:
    resp = session.post(
        f"{BASE_URL}/rl/environments/{ENV_ID}/step",
        json={"action": action},
    )
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()

done = False
while not done:
    obs = step({"type": "no_op", "parameters": {}})["obs"]
    wf = obs.get("warmup_factor", 1.0)   # 1.0 = fully warmed / no cold instance

    cpu = obs["cpu_util"]

    effective_cpu = cpu / wf if wf > 0 else cpu

    if effective_cpu > 0.75:
        action = {"type": "scale_out", "parameters": {"instanceCount": 1}}
    elif effective_cpu < 0.30 and obs["instances"] > 1:
        action = {"type": "scale_in", "parameters": {"instanceCount": 1}}
    else:
        action = {"type": "no_op", "parameters": {}}

    data = step(action)
    done = data["done"]
    print(
        f"  t={data['t']:4d}  wf={wf:.2f}  "
        f"cpu={cpu:.1%}  effective_cpu={effective_cpu:.1%}  "
        f"reward={data['reward']:+.3f}  done={done}"
    )

post.summary: Execute multiple actions in a single request
post.description:
Executes up to 30 actions sequentially in a single HTTP round-trip, advancing the
simulation by one step per action. Stops early and returns partial results if the
episode ends (`done: true`) before all actions are processed.

**Rate limiting:** Each action in the batch counts as one call against the
5 000 req/hr RL training quota. A batch of 30 actions consumes 30 quota units.
If the quota is exhausted mid-batch, the endpoint returns 429 with a `Retry-After`
header indicating how many seconds remain until the window resets.

**Idle TTL:** The last successful batch-step call resets the environment's 2-hour
idle timer, the same as a single `step` call.

post.summary: Submit an eval-episode job (async by default; ?sync=true for inline)
post.description:
Replays one or more ordered action sequences through a fresh episode reset and returns
per-episode cumulative rewards computed with `evalCostOverrides` applied. Use this to
detect **reward blind spots**: policies trained without egress or cross-AZ cost pricing
will show a significant reward drop (reward_collapse) when those dimensions are priced.

The endpoint does **not** mutate any stored environment or simulation state — all
episode rollouts are in-memory and ephemeral.

**Async mode (default):** Returns `202 Accepted` immediately with a `jobId`. Poll
`GET /rl/environments/{environmentId}/eval-episodes/{jobId}` until `status` is
`completed` or `failed`.

**Sync mode (`?sync=true`):** Runs the rollout in-process and returns the full result
inline with `200 OK`. Suitable for small workloads (≤ 3 episodes, ≤ 20 steps each).

**reward_collapse logic:** `reward_collapse` is `true` when
`meanEvalReward < trainingTotalReward − collapseThreshold × |trainingTotalReward|`.
With the default threshold of 0.20, any policy whose eval reward is more than 20 %
below its training reward is flagged as collapsing.

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://your-production-domain.com/api"
API_KEY = "your-api-key"
ENV_ID = "env-aws-001"

resp = requests.post(
    f"{BASE_URL}/rl/environments/{ENV_ID}/eval-episodes",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"},
    json={
        "actions": [
            [{"type": "no_op", "parameters": {}}] * 10
        ],
        "evalCostOverrides": {"egress": 0.5, "cross_az_traffic": 0.3},
        "collapseThreshold": 0.20,
    },
)
resp.raise_for_status()
data = resp.json()
print(f"reward_collapse={data['reward_collapse']}  mean_eval={data['meanEvalReward']:.3f}  training={data['trainingTotalReward']:.3f}")

post.summary: Run a chaos engineering test
post.description:
Execute a chaos engineering test by injecting failures into a simulation.
Can use pre-built scenarios or custom failure injections.

This endpoint works with simulations built on **any supported provider**,
including AWS, GCP, Azure, OCI, and **DigitalOcean**. When targeting a
DigitalOcean-based simulation, failure types such as `kill_instance`
affect Droplets, `zone_failure` targets DigitalOcean datacenter regions,
and `database_crash` targets Managed Database clusters.

**Failure naming surfaces** — three zone-related names, three different contexts:
- `zone_outage` — custom injection type in `customInjections[].failureType` (this endpoint)
- `az_outage` — failure type in the synchronous `POST /simulations/{id}/failures` API
- `zone_failure` — pre-built scenario ID used in `scenarioId`

**Multi-fault cascade example** — inject a zone outage and a database slowdown simultaneously
via `customInjections` to test correlated failure handling:

```json
{
  "simulationId": "sim-abc123",
  "customInjections": [
    { "failureType": "zone_outage", "targetZone": "us-east-1a", "duration": 120 },
    { "failureType": "database_slowdown", "targetResourceId": "db-primary", "intensity": 80, "duration": 120 }
  ]
}
```

**Resilience grade caveat** — the `grade` in the result reflects a static vulnerability
analysis of your architecture (SPOF detection, redundancy gaps). It may not change between
a single-fault run and a multi-fault run on already-resilient topologies because the grade
measures architectural exposure, not live error rate. To measure severity differences between
fault combinations, pair `POST /chaos/run` (vulnerability report) with the synchronous
`POST /simulations/{id}/failures` + step-loop pattern (live metrics).

post.summary: Explore multi-cloud deployment strategies
post.description:
Analyze a workload profile and generate optimized multi-cloud deployment strategies.
The system evaluates different provider combinations across AWS, GCP, Azure, OCI, and DigitalOcean
based on cost, latency, and vendor lock-in considerations.

**DigitalOcean as a candidate provider:** DigitalOcean is a first-class candidate in every
exploration run. It is particularly well-suited for cost-optimized workloads — Droplets and
Managed Databases typically produce the lowest monthly spend in the comparison report. Set a
high `cost` weight (e.g. 0.7+) and a moderate budget to see DigitalOcean-primary strategies
appear at the top of `topStrategies` in the results.

**Request body fields:** The request body has two top-level fields that are independent of
each other. `workloadProfile` describes the workload being evaluated (compute/database
instances, traffic, latency requirements, and primary region). `optimizationWeights` is a
separate top-level object — **not** nested inside `workloadProfile` — that controls how
strategies are ranked: `cost` (default 0.4), `latency` (default 0.4), and `vendorLockIn`
(default 0.2). Weights need not sum to 1.0; the engine normalises them during scoring. A
cost-heavy weight (e.g. `cost: 0.9`) surfaces the cheapest strategies at the top of
`topStrategies`; a latency-heavy weight (e.g. `latency: 0.9`) surfaces the lowest-latency
strategies instead.

Retrieve the **final** results from a multi-cloud exploration job.

**Only returns data once the job has finished.** This endpoint returns

sorted by `metrics.compositeScore` descending) and `allStrategies` (every strategy
evaluated, also sorted). Do **not** use the field names `variants`, `strategies`, or
`ranked` — those do not exist in the response.

# Multi-Cloud Strategy Comparison Report

## Winner: DigitalOcean AMD NVMe Primary Strategy

Monthly cost: **$6,200** — 55% lower than the AWS-dominant baseline ($13,800).
Average latency: **52 ms** — within the 150 ms SLA requirement.
Vendor lock-in score: **44/100** — low lock-in, easy to migrate if requirements change.

## Key Resources

- **Compute:** DigitalOcean AMD NVMe Droplets (s-2vcpu-4gb-amd, nyc3) — AMD EPYC processors with NVMe-backed local SSD storage deliver higher disk I/O throughput than standard Intel Droplets at the same hourly rate ($0.036/hr per Droplet). Ideal for workloads with frequent local reads/writes or ephemeral scratch space.
- **Database:** DigitalOcean Managed Databases (PostgreSQL, 2-node HA cluster, nyc3) — automated failover, daily backups, and PgBouncer connection pooling included at no extra charge.
- **Object Storage:** DigitalOcean Spaces — S3-compatible API, 250 GB included, optional CDN edge caching.

## AMD NVMe vs Standard Droplets

The `s-2vcpu-4gb-amd` slug selects the AMD NVMe variant of the standard shared-CPU tier. Compared to the equivalent Intel Droplet (`s-2vcpu-4gb`):
- Same vCPU count and RAM
- Same hourly price
- NVMe local SSD instead of spinning disk — up to 3× higher sequential read throughput
- AMD EPYC "Milan" or "Rome" core depending on host availability

Choose the AMD NVMe variant when your workload is I/O-bound (e.g. log processing, local caching, build pipelines) or when you want deterministic low-latency disk access without paying for a dedicated CPU plan.

| Metric | DO AMD NVMe Primary | DO AMD NVMe + GCP | AWS-Dominant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monthly cost | $6,200 | $8,100 | $13,800 |
| Avg latency | 52 ms | 49 ms | 41 ms |
| Lock-in score | 44 | 38 | 74 |

## Recommendation

For cost-sensitive workloads with moderate I/O requirements, the DigitalOcean AMD NVMe Primary strategy delivers the best value. The 11 ms latency gap versus the AWS baseline is unlikely to affect end-user experience for the given SLA. If burst capacity beyond current Droplet limits is anticipated, consider the DO AMD NVMe + GCP Balanced strategy, which adds only $1,900/month for a 3 ms latency improvement and lower vendor lock-in.

get.summary: Get partial multi-cloud exploration results while a job is running
get.description:
Retrieve strategies accumulated so far for a multi-cloud exploration job, even while the job is still running.

This endpoint is the dedicated channel for polling partial results during job execution.
The `/results` endpoint requires the job to be completed; use this endpoint instead when you want
to start analyzing strategies before the full exploration finishes.

**Polling pattern:**
```
while true:
  data = GET /api/multi-cloud/jobs/{jobId}/partial-results
  show data.allStrategies to user
  if data.isComplete: break
  sleep(2s)
full = GET /api/multi-cloud/jobs/{jobId}/results
```

**isComplete flag:**
- `false` — job is still `pending` or `running`; more strategies may arrive
- `true` — job has reached a terminal state (`completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled`)

**When `isComplete` is true and `status` is `completed`**, fetch the ranked
`topStrategies` and `comparisonReport` from `GET /api/multi-cloud/jobs/{jobId}/results`.

x-codeSamples.label: curl
x-codeSamples.source:
while true; do
  DATA=$(curl -s "https://your-production-domain.com/api/multi-cloud/jobs/job_abc123/partial-results" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY")
  echo "$DATA" | jq '{strategies: (.allStrategies | length), isComplete: .isComplete}'
  [ "$(echo "$DATA" | jq -r '.isComplete')" = "true" ] && break
  sleep 2
done

specified DigitalOcean Droplet size tier (e.g. `s-2vcpu-4gb`,

This endpoint is only valid for DigitalOcean-provider simulations;

get.summary: Validate simulation cost accuracy against provider benchmarks
get.description:
Compares the simulation's cost estimates against known real-world provider
pricing benchmarks. Returns a validation result indicating whether the
simulated cost per hour is within the acceptable tolerance (±10%).

Useful for confirming the simulation is faithfully modelling provider
pricing before using it for cost-optimisation decisions.

**Skip semantics:** Resources without a `serviceFamily` characteristic,
or whose `provider`/`serviceFamily`/`size` combination has no pricing
benchmark entry, are silently skipped. When all resources are skipped,
`validations` is empty, `summary.total` is `0`, and `checked` is `false`.
In that state `valid: true` means "no failures among the zero resources
checked" — it does **not** mean the simulation's cost accuracy was
verified. Always check `checked: true` before acting on `valid`.

Requires `read` scope and ownership.

valid.description: Whether all checked resources are within the ±10% cost tolerance. Only meaningful when `checked` is `true`.

checked.description: `true` when at least one resource had a matching pricing benchmark and was evaluated. `false` means no comparable data was found — the simulation resources may lack `serviceFamily` or have no pricing benchmark entry. When `checked` is `false`, `valid: true` does **not** mean accuracy was verified.

source.description: Source citation for the benchmark value

total.description: Number of resources that had a matching benchmark

avgDeviation.description: Average deviation across all checked resources

skippedCount.description: Number of resources (or resource-metric pairs) that were evaluated but had no matching benchmark entry and were therefore skipped.

skippedReasons.description: Human-readable explanation for each skipped resource. Common reasons: no `serviceFamily` set, or no pricing benchmark found for the provider/serviceFamily/size combination.

get.summary: Validate simulation performance accuracy against provider benchmarks
get.description:
Compares the simulation's throughput and latency estimates against known
real-world provider benchmarks. Returns a validation result indicating
whether the simulated performance metrics are within the acceptable
tolerance (±15%).

**Skip semantics:** Resources without a `serviceFamily` characteristic
are skipped entirely. For resources that do have a `serviceFamily`,
individual metrics (`max_throughput`, `baseline_latency`,
`max_connections`) are skipped when no benchmark entry exists for that
provider/metric combination. When all resource-metric pairs are skipped,
`validations` is empty, `summary.total` is `0`, and `checked` is `false`.
In that state `valid: true` means "no failures among the zero pairs
checked" — it does **not** mean the simulation's performance accuracy
was verified. Always check `checked: true` before acting on `valid`.

Requires `read` scope and ownership.

valid.description: Whether all checked resource-metric pairs are within the ±15% performance tolerance. Only meaningful when `checked` is `true`.

checked.description: `true` when at least one resource-metric pair had a matching performance benchmark and was evaluated. `false` means no comparable data was found — the simulation resources may lack `serviceFamily`, or no performance benchmark exists for the provider/metric combination. When `checked` is `false`, `valid: true` does **not** mean accuracy was verified.

metric.description: The metric that was validated. One of: `max_throughput`, `baseline_latency`, `max_connections`.

total.description: Number of resource-metric pairs that had a matching benchmark

skippedCount.description: Number of resource-metric pairs that were skipped because no benchmark was found.

skippedReasons.description: Human-readable explanation for each skipped resource-metric pair.

get.summary: Validate both cost and performance accuracy
get.description:
Convenience endpoint that runs both cost and performance accuracy
validations in a single call. Returns a combined result with an
`overallValid` flag that is `true` only if both checks pass.

Requires `read` scope and ownership.

cost.description: Full cost accuracy validation result — same shape as `GET /validate-cost-accuracy`. Check `cost.checked` before trusting `cost.valid`.

post.summary: Submit async AI analysis job
post.description:
Creates an async AI analysis job for a simulation. Immediately returns a
`jobId` (HTTP 202) so callers are never blocked by the ~11 s gateway
timeout. Supported job types:

- `explain` — natural-language explanation of simulation behaviour
- `troubleshoot` — diagnosis and remediation steps for a described issue
- `analyze_bottlenecks` — ranked bottleneck detection with remediation
- `optimize` — infrastructure optimisation suggestions

**Poll flow:**
1. `POST /api/ai-jobs` → receive `jobId`
2. `GET /api/ai-jobs/{jobId}` → poll until `status` is `completed`
3. `GET /api/ai-jobs/{jobId}/results` → retrieve the AI output

**Authentication:** Required. Provide `Authorization: Bearer cwm_live_…`
or an x402 payment header with call type `ai_analysis`.

issue.description: Required for troubleshoot — describe the problem

Returns the current status of an async AI analysis job. Poll until
`status` is `completed` (or `failed`/`cancelled`), then call
`GET /ai-jobs/{jobId}/results` to retrieve the AI output.

**Authentication:** Required (API key, read scope).

Cancels a pending or running AI analysis job. Idempotent — cancelling
an already-terminal job returns 200 with the terminal state.

**Authentication:** Required (API key, write scope).

Retrieves the full AI output for a completed job. Returns HTTP 400 if

- `troubleshoot` → `{ guidance: string }`
- `analyze_bottlenecks` → `{ analysis: string, doRecommendation: string|null }`
- `optimize` → `{ suggestions: string }`

**Authentication:** Required (API key, read scope).

type.description: Resource type. `kubernetes` models a managed container node pool (EKS / GKE / AKS / OKE / DOKS): its `characteristics.nodeCount` worker nodes autoscale between `characteristics.minNodes` and `characteristics.maxNodes`, growing both serving capacity (`maxThroughput`) and hourly cost proportionally.

serviceFamily.description: Provider-specific service family identifier. AWS values include: `ec2`, `rds`, `aurora-postgresql`, `aurora-dsql`, `aurora-serverless`, `dynamodb`, `s3`, `elb`, `cloudfront`, `lambda`. GCP values include: `gce`, `cloud-sql`, `cloud-spanner`, `bigtable-ssd`, `bigtable-hdd`, `cloud-run`, `gcs`, `cloud-load-balancing`. Azure values include: `azure_vm`, `azure-sql`, `azure-functions`, `blob-storage`, `azure-lb`, `eventhub`. OCI values include: `oci_vm`, `autonomous-db`, `oci-container`, `oci-lb`, `oci-streaming`. DigitalOcean values include: `droplets`, `managed_postgresql`, `spaces`, `load_balancer`.

maxConnections.description: Database only — the connection-pool capacity (maximum concurrent connections) for a database resource. The simulation models connection-pool pressure as `activeConnections / maxConnections` (surfaced as `metrics.connection_pressure`), so raising this value gives the database more headroom before the pool saturates. Defaults to 100 when omitted.

capacityGB.description: Storage only — provisioned storage capacity in gigabytes for a storage/volume resource. Used together with `maxIops` to model block-storage throughput and IOPS utilization.

maxIops.description: Storage only — the provisioned maximum IOPS (I/O operations per second) for a block-storage volume. The simulation models storage IOPS utilization against this ceiling (surfaced as `metrics.storageIopsUtilization`). Falls back to the provider's default volume profile IOPS when omitted.

cacheHitRate.description: Cache / CDN only — the expected cache hit rate as a fraction between 0 and 1 (e.g. `0.85` = 85%). Higher values reduce the load that reaches downstream origin/database resources and lower effective latency. Defaults to 0.8 when omitted for cache resources.

autoscaling.description: Compute only — marks a compute resource as the autoscaling primary. When multiple compute resources exist, the engine uses the one flagged `autoscaling: true` as the autoscaling target; otherwise it falls back to the first compute resource.

maxInstances.description: Compute only — hard per-resource ceiling for RL `scale_out` actions. When set, the effective maximum is `min(autoscalingConfig.maxInstances, characteristics.maxInstances)`, giving individual compute resources a tighter cap than the simulation-wide autoscaling config. Ignored on non-compute resource types.

minInstances.description: Compute only — hard per-resource floor for RL `scale_in` actions. When set, the effective minimum is `max(autoscalingConfig.minInstances, characteristics.minInstances)`, preventing scale-in below this floor even when the simulation-wide autoscaling config would allow it. Ignored on non-compute resource types.

nodeCount.description: Kubernetes only — the current number of worker nodes in the managed node pool. The cluster's `maxThroughput` and hourly cost scale proportionally with this count as autoscaling adds/removes nodes.

minNodes.description: Kubernetes only — the minimum number of worker nodes the node pool will scale in to. Defaults to the provider autoscaling profile minimum when omitted.

maxNodes.description: Kubernetes only — the maximum number of worker nodes the node pool will scale out to. Defaults to the provider autoscaling profile maximum when omitted.

pricingModel.description: Compute and Kubernetes only — the pricing model for worker instances. `on-demand` (default) uses standard pay-as-you-go rates. `spot` applies the provider's spot/preemptible discount to reduce instance cost significantly (AWS/GCP/Azure: ~60% off on-demand; OCI: exactly 50% off) at the cost of potential interruption when the cloud provider needs capacity back. Non-compute resource types (database, storage, network, etc.) and DigitalOcean resources (which have no spot offering) ignore this field.

nodePools.description: Kubernetes only — multiple node pools per cluster. When present, each pool scales independently within its own min/max bounds and is billed at its own per-node hourly rate. The legacy single-pool fields (`nodeCount`, `minNodes`, `maxNodes`) are used only when `nodePools` is absent.

nodeCount.description: Current number of worker nodes in this pool. Scales proportionally with the pool's serving capacity and cost as autoscaling adds/removes nodes.

minNodes.description: Minimum number of worker nodes this pool will scale in to. Defaults to the provider autoscaling profile minimum when omitted.

maxNodes.description: Maximum number of worker nodes this pool will scale out to. Defaults to the provider autoscaling profile maximum when omitted.

perNodeRate.description: Hourly cost per node for this pool. Falls back to the provider default rate when omitted.

maxThroughput.description: Per-node serving capacity (requests/second) for this pool. When pools carry different instance sizes, the engine uses these values to compute the correct CPU credit on scale events — a pool of large nodes relieves more load per node added or removed than a pool of small nodes. Falls back to a uniform distribution of the cluster's total `maxThroughput` across all nodes when omitted (preserving backwards-compatible behaviour for homogeneous fleets).

streamShardsCount.description: DynamoDB only — number of shards provisioned for the DynamoDB Stream attached to this table. Each shard processes up to 1 000 records/s. When write throughput (see `streamWriteRps`) exceeds the total shard capacity, the simulation engine accumulates iterator age (seconds) and emits a `stream_lag` warning event. The iterator age is drained proportionally when traffic falls back within shard capacity. Ignored on non-DynamoDB resources.

streamWriteRps.description: DynamoDB only — explicit write throughput (records/s) for the DynamoDB Stream. When omitted the engine estimates write load as 10 % of the current simulation traffic. Providing an explicit value is useful when the stream write pattern is decoupled from the simulated request traffic (e.g. bulk imports or batch pipelines that run independently). Ignored when `streamShardsCount` is 0 or absent.

eventNotificationsEnabled.description: Storage event notifications — when true the engine models event notification delivery latency: baseline 1 500 ms, rising by 1 ms per 10 RPS above 5 000 RPS, capped at 30 000 ms. The latency penalty is propagated to downstream serverless compute resources (Lambda for S3, Cloud Functions for GCS, Azure Functions for Azure Blob via Event Grid, OCI Functions for OCI Object Storage). A `notification_delayed` warning event is emitted once when simulation traffic exceeds 20 000 RPS and cleared when traffic drops back below that threshold. Supported providers: `aws` (S3), `gcp` (GCS), `azure` (Blob Storage), `oci` (Object Storage). Ignored on non-storage resources and OCI block-volume resources.

partitionCount.description: Azure Event Hubs only — number of partitions provisioned on the event hub. Each partition processes up to `partitionWriteRps` write records/s (defaults to 1 000 records/s per partition when omitted). When write throughput exceeds total partition capacity the engine accumulates `partitionLag` (seconds) in resource metadata and emits a `partition_lag` warning event when lag exceeds 30 s. Ignored on non-eventhub resources.

streamPartitions.description: OCI Streaming only — number of stream partitions. Uses the same Kafka-style offset lag model as Azure Event Hubs `partitionCount`. When absent the engine falls back to `partitionCount`. A `stream_lag` warning event fires when lag exceeds 30 s. Ignored on non-oci-streaming resources.

partitionWriteRps.description: Azure Event Hubs / OCI Streaming only — total write records/second produced into the event stream by all upstream writers combined. When omitted the engine estimates write load as 10 % of the current simulation traffic. Each partition handles 1 000 records/s; lag accumulates when `partitionWriteRps` exceeds `partitionCount × 1 000` (Event Hubs) or `streamPartitions × 1 000` (OCI Streaming).

warmupSteps.description: Compute and Kubernetes only — length of the JIT/CPU warm-up window in simulation steps. The capacity penalty is steepest on the first step (counter 0) and decays linearly to zero once the counter reaches this value, after which the resource operates at full capacity. Falls back to the engine default of 3 when omitted. A longer window models runtimes that take many steps to reach full throughput (e.g. JVM + JIT compilation, Python ML model loading); a value of 1 produces a single-step burst followed immediately by full capacity (useful for static binaries or pre-warmed containers). Ignored on non-compute resource types.

warmupSeverity.description: Compute and Kubernetes only — peak fraction by which effective capacity is reduced on the first warm-up step. For example, `0.8` reduces capacity to 20 % of its normal value on step 0. The penalty decays linearly to 0 across the `warmupSteps` window. Falls back to the engine default of `0.5` (capacity halved) when omitted. Use higher values (closer to 1) to model cold-start-heavy stacks such as JVM applications or services that load large ML models at start; use lower values to model near-instant start-ups; set to `0` to disable the warm-up capacity penalty entirely. Ignored on non-compute resource types.

recoveryPolicy.description: Per-resource recovery thresholds that control how quickly the simulation transitions a resource from critical → warning → healthy. All four fields default to the global values (criticalCpuThreshold: 80, criticalSteps: 4, warningCpuThreshold: 70, warningSteps: 3) when omitted. Stateless microservices can use lower thresholds and fewer steps to heal faster; databases can use higher thresholds and more steps for a stricter recovery window.

criticalCpuThreshold.description: CPU must drop to or below this percentage before the critical → warning cooldown clock starts.

criticalSteps.description: Number of consecutive simulation steps the CPU must stay below criticalCpuThreshold before transitioning from critical to warning.

warningCpuThreshold.description: CPU must drop to or below this percentage before the warning → healthy cooldown clock starts.

warningSteps.description: Number of consecutive simulation steps the CPU must stay below warningCpuThreshold before transitioning from warning to healthy.

tick_seconds.description:
Number of simulated seconds each step advances the simulation clock.
Default is 60 (one simulated minute per step). Set higher values to
model longer time horizons (e.g. 300 for 5-minute ticks, 3600 for
hourly ticks). The value is fixed for the lifetime of the episode.

unmodeled_cost_penalty_per_dimension.description: Reward penalty applied per active unmodeled cost dimension per step. The total penalty is -(count × this value) and is reported in `reward_components.unmodeled_cost` and `unmodeled_cost_penalty` in the step response. Default is 0.1.

evalCostOverrides.description: Per-dimension cost override rates in USD per 1 000 RPS per hour. Supported keys: `egress` (outbound data-transfer fee charged whenever traffic > 0) and `cross_az_traffic` (inter-AZ data-transfer fee charged when resources in different Availability Zones are connected). When present, these rates are added to the simulated cost before computing the reward cost score, making previously unpriced dimensions visible in the reward signal. Primarily used by the `eval-episodes` endpoint to stress-test trained policies against real-world cost blind spots.

RLTradeoffSummary.description:
Per-metric deltas between the episode-start config and the episode-end config.
Returned only on the final step response (`done: true`). Use this to evaluate
whether the agent's actions improved cost, latency, and resilience over the course
of the episode.

costDeltaPercent.description: Cost change as a percentage of the episode-start cost. Negative = cheaper.

costDirection.description: improved = lower cost, degraded = higher cost. Unchanged when |delta| < 0.5%.

latencyP95DeltaMs.description: P95 latency change in milliseconds relative to episode start. Negative = faster.

latencyP95Direction.description: improved = lower latency, degraded = higher latency. Unchanged when |delta| < 1 ms.

resilienceDeltaScore.description: Change in resilience score (uptime = 1 − error_rate) between episode start and end. Range −1 to 1. Positive = more resilient (fewer errors).

resilienceDirection.description: improved = higher uptime, degraded = lower uptime. Unchanged when |delta| < 0.001.

createdAt.description: ISO 8601 timestamp when the job was created

episodes.description: Per-episode results in the same order as the request `actions` array

episodeIndex.description: Zero-based index of this episode in the request array

due to inactivity. Computed as `lastActivityAt` (or `createdAt` if no step
or reset has been called yet) plus the 2-hour idle TTL. Agents can use
this value to schedule keep-alive calls (`POST /rl/environments/{environmentId}/step`
or `POST /rl/environments/{environmentId}/reset`) before expiry.

RewardWeights.description:
User-defined weights controlling how cost, resilience, latency, performance,
and stability each contribute to the scalar reward returned on each RL step.

Valid create-time keys: `cost`, `resilience`, `latency`, `performance`, `stability`.
These are the weights you set when creating or resetting an environment — they
are distinct from the step-response `reward_components` fields
(`connection_pressure`, `unmodeled_cost`, `sla`) which are computed automatically.

All values must be non-negative. They are automatically normalized to sum to 1.0
on the server side, so you may supply raw priority scores
(e.g. `{ cost: 3, resilience: 1, latency: 1 }`) or pre-normalized fractions
(e.g. `{ cost: 0.6, resilience: 0.2, latency: 0.2 }`).

When omitted (the default), the agent uses the built-in weighting of
latency: 0.35 / cost: 0.25 / resilience: 0.40 — optimized for
balanced cloud workloads.

cost.description: Weight assigned to cost optimization (staying within cost budget).

resilience.description: Weight assigned to resilience (low error rates, stable resources, no SLA violations).

latency.description: Weight assigned to latency performance (p95 latency relative to SLA target).

performance.description: Weight assigned to throughput and capacity performance.

stability.description: Weight assigned to autoscaling stability (penalizes thrashing and rapid oscillation).

instanceCount.description: Number of instances to add (`scale_out`) or remove (`scale_in`) — a delta, not a target count. The effective change is clamped to the per-resource instance bounds: the ceiling is `min(autoscalingConfig.maxInstances, characteristics.maxInstances)` for `scale_out`, and the floor is `max(autoscalingConfig.minInstances, characteristics.minInstances)` for `scale_in`. When clamping occurs the step response `info` object contains the flat keys `scale_clamped: true`, `requested` (this parameter's value), `actual` (delta applied, 0 if blocked), and `limit` (effective bound).

**Per-resource form** — provide `resourceId` and the nested `recoveryPolicy`

**Global flat form** — omit `resourceId` and pass the four threshold fields
(`criticalCpuThreshold`, `criticalSteps`, `warningCpuThreshold`, `warningSteps`)

flat fields if both are supplied.

warmup_factor.description:
Minimum warmup capacity factor across all compute/Kubernetes resources that carry a warm-up counter, in (0, 1]. Value is 1.0 when all instances are fully warmed; less than 1.0 while any instance is still in its warm-up window.

**Mid-episode transition:** This field is absent at episode start when no compute resource carries a warm-up counter. It appears dynamically once a cold compute instance is provisioned — either via an `add_resource` action or via canvas autoscaling triggered by high CPU or traffic. After the warm-up window completes (typically 3 steps), the field returns to 1.0 and may become absent again if no further cold instances exist.

**Safe access pattern:** Agents building a fixed-width observation vector must guard against its absence by defaulting to 1.0 when the field is not present. In Python: `wf = obs.get("warmup_factor", 1.0)`. In JavaScript/TypeScript: `const wf = obs.warmup_factor ?? 1.0`. Never assume the field is present across all steps of an episode.

Use this as a direct observation feature in your reward function — low values indicate recently-provisioned instances are not yet at full throughput. For per-resource detail see metrics.compute[].warmup_factor.

RLMetrics.description: Evaluation-oriented metrics returned alongside obs by the step and observation endpoints. These are the outputs your reward function and monitoring dashboards should read. Fractions (error_rate, uptime) are in the range [0, 1]. The `connection_pressure` field is optional — it is only present when the simulation contains at least one database resource (e.g. RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure SQL, Autonomous DB, Managed PostgreSQL). Agents should guard against its absence when no database resource is configured.

sla_violations.description: Number of SLA dimension violations at this step (0 = fully compliant)

connection_pressure.description: DB connection-pool pressure ratio (activeConnections / maxConnections), capped at 3.0. Only present when the simulation contains database resources. Values > 1.0 indicate pool exhaustion; values > 1.5 indicate severe saturation. Use this field to build reward functions that penalise connection-pool exhaustion independently of the aggregate error_rate signal.

compute.description:
Per-resource warm-up state for compute and Kubernetes resources that carry a warm-up counter. Only present when at least one such resource exists in the simulation. Absent when no resources have a warm-up counter.

**Mid-episode transition:** Like `obs.warmup_factor`, this array is absent at episode start when no compute resource carries a warm-up counter. It appears dynamically once a cold compute instance is provisioned mid-episode (via `add_resource` or canvas autoscaling) and disappears again once all warm-up windows complete. Guard against its absence with `metrics.compute ?? []` or `metrics.get("compute", [])`.

Agents should read `obs.warmup_factor` as the primary scalar observation feature — do not re-derive it from step counters or this array.

skuClass.description:
Primary product-class label for this allocation. Derived from the two per-dimension fields below (`computeSkuClass`, `databaseSkuClass`) using the following precedence: if `computeSkuClass` is non-default (i.e. `do-droplet`, `bare-metal-compute`, or `free-tier-compute`), that compute class is used even when a `databaseSkuClass` is also present. Otherwise the `databaseSkuClass` is used when present; the final fallback is `general-compute`.
Allocations that share the same `skuClass` are cost-comparable at the class level; allocations with different values are not directly comparable — see the parent Strategy's `crossClassNote` when present.

computeSkuClass.description:
Compute-dimension SKU class for this allocation.
`general-compute` — standard dedicated-vCPU VMs (EC2, Compute Engine, Azure VMs, OCI VM.Standard/Flex; the default when no specific compute family is set), `do-droplet` — DigitalOcean Droplets (shared-vCPU cloud VMs; different resource model and performance guarantees from dedicated-vCPU instances), `free-tier-compute` — always-free / zero-cost compute (OCI Always Free AMD micro VMs; costs excluded from estimate totals), `bare-metal-compute` — dedicated bare-metal servers (OCI BM.Standard3.64, BM.Optimized3.36; no hypervisor overhead, full core isolation).
Always present after annotation; defaults to `general-compute`.

databaseSkuClass.description:
Database-dimension SKU class for this allocation. Absent when no database service family is set (allocation carries no bespoke database tier).
`managed-rdbms` — provisioned relational databases (RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure SQL, …), `oci-heatwave` — OCI MySQL HeatWave DB System and HeatWave Analytics Cluster (in-memory analytics accelerator; distinct billing model and capability profile from standard managed-rdbms — not directly cost-comparable), `serverless-db` — pay-per-use / auto-scaling databases (Aurora Serverless, Cloud Spanner, Autonomous DB, …), `managed-nosql` — wide-column or key-value NoSQL (Bigtable SSD/HDD, …).

databaseCostPerHour.description: Hourly database cost for this provider slice (USD)

storageCostPerHour.description: Hourly storage cost for this provider slice (USD)

egressCostPerHour.description: Hourly internet egress cost attributed to this provider slice (USD), after deducting the provider's free monthly egress allowance (converted to an hourly GB budget — ÷ 730). Free allowances: OCI 10,000 GB/month (Always Free, flat), DigitalOcean 1,000 GB/instance/month (scales with computeInstances), AWS 100 GB/month, GCP 200 GB/month (Americas), Azure 5 GB/month. Volume within the free tier produces zero. Zero also when trafficRPS is 0.

totalCostPerHour.description: Sum of compute + database + storage + egress costs for this slice (USD)

computeInstances.description: Number of compute instances in this provider slice

databaseInstances.description: Number of database instances in this provider slice

storageGB.description: Total storage provisioned in this provider slice (GB)

computeUnitRate.description: Per-instance hourly compute rate used for this slice (USD/hr)

databaseUnitRate.description: Per-instance hourly database rate used for this slice (USD/hr)

storageUnitRate.description: Per-GB storage rate used (USD/GB/hr, on a per-1000-GB basis)

egressFreeTierExhaustedAtRPS.description: The requests-per-second (RPS) threshold at which this provider's hourly egress free-tier allowance is fully consumed, given the current traffic share and instance count. Below this value egressCostPerHour is $0; above it the overage rate applies. Computed as Math.round(freeHourlyGB / (RPS_TO_GB_PER_HOUR × share)), where RPS_TO_GB_PER_HOUR = 0.0072 and freeHourlyGB = monthlyFreeGB / 730 (DigitalOcean scales by computeInstances). Omitted when trafficPercentage is 0 or when the provider has no free egress allowance.

databaseServiceFamily.description: Database product sub-family override applied to this slice (e.g. "cloud-sql", "aurora-serverless", "autonomous-db"). Absent when the provider's default managed database rate is used.

totalCostPerHour.description: Total hourly cost across all providers

vendorLockInScore.description: Vendor lock-in score (0-100, higher = more locked in / harder to migrate away). Single-provider strategies score 55-84 depending on service proprietary-ness (Aurora Serverless scores higher than standard RDS); multi-provider strategies score 20-50 depending on traffic distribution and provider count.

dataPortabilityScore.description: Data portability score (0-100, higher = more portable)

migrationEgressCost.description: One-time data-migration egress cost estimate (USD) — the cost of moving the workload's stored data out of the source provider. Computed as `EGRESS_PER_GB_RATES[sourceProvider] × storageGB`. Always present; zero-valued strategies have zero storage in the workload profile.

egressCostPerHour.description: Estimated ongoing internet egress cost per hour (USD) — the recurring cost of serving outbound responses to external users. Derived from `trafficRPS` using a 2 KB average response payload (RPS × 3600 s/hr × 0.000002 GB/request) and each provider's `INTERNET_EGRESS_RATES` overage rate (USD/GB), after deducting each provider's free monthly egress allowance (converted to an hourly GB budget): OCI 10,000 GB/month (Always Free, flat), DigitalOcean 1,000 GB/instance/month (scales with computeInstances), AWS 100 GB/month, GCP 200 GB/month (Americas), Azure 5 GB/month. For multi-provider strategies the cost is traffic-share-weighted across all allocations. This estimate is added into `totalCostPerHour` so rankings reflect the full ongoing cost including egress. Absent only on strategies with zero traffic. Volume within a provider's free tier produces `egressCostPerHour: 0`.

latencyHeadroomPct.description: How far below the user's latency SLO this strategy sits, expressed as a percentage of the SLO limit. Computed as max(0, (SLO − p95LatencyMs) / SLO × 100). A value of 13.75 means p95 latency is 13.75% below the SLO limit — the strategy has that much buffer before it would breach the target. 0 means the strategy is at or above the SLO limit. Absent for strategies that exceed the SLO.

Strategy.description: A flight-simulator-style planning estimate for a specific multi-cloud deployment configuration. Cost and latency figures reflect baseline on-demand rates under typical load and are **not actual billing data**. Internet egress is estimated and included in `totalCostPerHour` via the `egressCostPerHour` field in each `costBreakdown` entry, after deducting each provider's free monthly egress allowance (OCI 10,000 GB/month, DigitalOcean 1,000 GB/instance/month, AWS 100 GB/month, GCP 200 GB/month, Azure 5 GB/month). Still excluded: monitoring/support surcharges, non-egress free-tier credits, reserved-instance discounts, and spot/preemptible pricing. Allocations with different `skuClass` values are not directly cost-comparable; the `crossClassNote` field explains any such mix. Validate top candidates by materialising them as owned simulations before making infrastructure commitments.

crossClassNote.description: Present only when this strategy's allocations span more than one class in either the compute dimension (comparing `computeSkuClass` values) or the database dimension (comparing `databaseSkuClass` values). Each dimension is evaluated independently so a compute-tier mismatch is never masked by a shared database tier, and vice-versa. The note names the mismatched dimension(s) and warns that cost and latency figures across those allocations may not be directly comparable because they model different product tiers. Absent when all allocations share the same class in both dimensions.

No credentials provided to an API-key-protected endpoint. The response
body includes a machine-readable `apiKeyAuth` block pointing to the key
creation endpoint so agents can self-serve an API key without consulting

X402PaymentRequired.description:
Payment required — the endpoint is metered and no API key was provided.

The response body follows the [x402 v2 protocol](https://x402.org) and describes
the USDC-on-Base payment that the caller must make before retrying the request.
After paying, re-send the original request with a `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE` header containing
the signed payment payload.  The server will verify the payment against the
PayAI facilitator at `https://facilitator.payai.network`.

The `PAYMENT-REQUIRED` response header carries this entire JSON body as a
base64-encoded string for protocol-aware clients.

Call `GET /api/billing/x402/config` to retrieve the current price table and wallet
address before constructing a payment.

BearerAuth.description:
API key authentication using Bearer tokens in the Authorization header.

**How to authenticate:**
1. Create an API key using POST /api/keys
2. Include the key in the Authorization header: `Bearer cwm_live_<your_key>`
3. All RL environment endpoints require authentication

**Rate Limits:**
- Default: 1000 requests/hour per key
- Configurable per key
- Returns 429 when exceeded

x402.name: PAYMENT-SIGNATURE
x402.description:
x402 v2 micropayment protocol. Agents send a signed USDC micro-payment
on the Base network in the `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE` header and get full
access to the metered endpoint in a single round-trip — no account,
no API key, no sign-up required.

**402 → pay → retry loop:**
1. Call the endpoint without a `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE` header.
2. Receive a `402 Payment Required` response. The body is a
   standard JSON `PaymentRequired` object. The same payload is also
   echoed as a base64-encoded string in the `PAYMENT-REQUIRED`
   response header for clients that cannot access the body.
3. Decode the `PaymentRequired` body (or the `PAYMENT-REQUIRED`
   header) to read the exact `payTo` wallet,
   USDC amount, network, and facilitator URL.
4. Construct and sign the payment with your x402 client library.
5. Retry the request with the `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE` header — the server
   verifies via `https://facilitator.payai.network` and responds `200`.

**Discovery:** `GET /api/billing/x402/config` returns the live `payTo`
address, per-call-type USDC amounts, facilitator URL, and the
credits-per-USDC conversion rate. Always fetch this before hardcoding
any amounts.

**Price range:** $0.0010 per step/RL call — $0.0050 per
analysis/chaos/multi-cloud call (see `x-x402-price-usdc` on each
operation for the exact amount).

**Facilitator:** `https://facilitator.payai.network` (PayAI-operated,
settles on Base mainnet).
